name: IT incident management: one incident through an ITIL-style service desk
summary: This process restores normal service for one IT incident reported by an employee or raised by monitoring. The service desk logs, categorises and tries to fix it; about a third of incidents are routed to second-line resolver groups, and a smaller share to third-line engineers or a vendor, sometimes needing an approved change. A rare major incident follows a separate path with a bridge, updates and a review. Elapsed time is dominated by group queues, waits for users and vendors, change windows and the confirmation period before closure, and it grows with misrouting and reassignment between groups.

baseline.org_archetype: The internal IT function of a 5,000-employee organisation with an in-house service desk, second-line support groups, third-line engineering teams and outside vendors, all working in one ITSM tool.
baseline.notes: Incidents only; service requests, problems and standard changes are separate processes.

trigger: An employee reports a fault by phone, portal, email or chat, or monitoring raises an alert that the service desk logs.
end_state: The incident is closed after confirmation or automatic closure, closed after the user stops responding, or the major incident review is complete.

volume.seasonality: Peaks on Monday mornings, after large releases and at the start of each month; lower in holiday weeks.

evidence.note: About 0.8 tickets per user per month for 5,000 users, of which about half are incidents rather than requests. HDI reports desktop volumes of 0.54 to 1.38 tickets per seat per month; the incident share is an author estimate.

systems.name: IT service management tool (incident, problem and change records, SLA clocks)
Knowledge base and known error database
Service desk telephony and call distribution
Remote control and endpoint management tool

steps.name: Log incident and verify caller
steps.description: The service desk analyst answers the call, chat or portal ticket, verifies the caller's identity, links the affected device or service from the configuration database and types a description of the symptom and its business impact into a new incident record.
inputs: user call, email or portal form

error.defect_description: Vague description or wrong configuration item, which slows diagnosis and routing.

control.basis: Information security policy: verify identity before account or access changes

evidence.note: Logging is an ITIL sub-process; phone calls are answered in minutes while portal and email tickets queue, so the wait is an author estimate.

steps.name: Categorise and set priority
steps.description: The analyst picks a category and subcategory, rates impact and urgency to derive the priority from the matrix, and checks the open major incidents to see whether this is part of a known outage.
outputs: categorised incident with priority and SLA clock

error.defect_description: Wrong category or priority, causing misrouting or a missed SLA.

control.basis: ITSM policy and service level agreements: impact by urgency priority matrix sets response and resolution targets

next.condition: widespread outage or critical service down

evidence.note: Matrix and targets are stated in a published ITSM guideline; the share of major incidents is an author estimate.

steps.name: Search knowledge base
steps.description: The analyst searches the knowledge base and known error records using the symptom and error text, and opens any matching article or workaround.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common ITIL service desk practice in large organisations, 2019 to 2022.

steps.name: First-line diagnosis and fix
steps.description: The analyst works the issue with the user, often through remote control: resets passwords, clears caches, repairs configuration or applies a documented workaround, then records what was done. If the fix is outside first-line skills or access, the analyst prepares to escalate.

error.defect_description: Symptom fixed but not the cause, so the user reopens.

next.condition: needs information or action from the user

evidence.note: Average first level resolution was 61.4% to 77.8% (HDI, 2017); 60% here plus returns after user replies gives about 65%, since incidents are harder than service requests.

steps.name: Wait for user information (first line)
steps.description: The ticket is set to a wait-user status while the user supplies a screenshot, error code or a time for a remote session. The analyst sends up to three reminders before closing a silent ticket.

evidence.note: The wait-user substatus and the question of its misuse come from the Volvo IT log; durations and shares are author estimates.

steps.name: Route to resolver group
steps.description: The analyst chooses the second-line assignment group from the category and configuration item, writes handover notes on what was tried, and reassigns the incident. Re-routing after a wrong assignment also passes through here.

next.condition: sits unaccepted until the SLA warning fires

evidence.note: Functional escalation to second line is an ITIL sub-process; the misrouting rate is an author estimate.

steps.name: Second-line triage and acceptance
steps.description: An engineer in the resolver group picks the incident from the group queue, reads the notes and history, and accepts it, passes it to another group or sends it back to the service desk as something first line should resolve.

evidence.note: 17.8% of desktop support tickets were level 1 capable (HDI); each reassignment costs users 1 hour 38 minutes (HappySignals). Queue time and branch shares are author estimates.

steps.name: Second-line diagnosis
steps.description: The engineer reviews logs, monitoring and recent changes for the configuration item, reproduces the fault or connects to the device, and decides on a fix, a wait for the user, or escalation to third line.

error.defect_description: Misdiagnosis leads to a fix that does not hold.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common ITIL service desk practice in large organisations, 2019 to 2022.

steps.name: Apply fix or workaround
steps.description: The engineer applies the fix: reconfigures software, restores access, replaces a part or visits the desk, and tests with the user where possible. Fixes that alter production systems need a change record.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common ITIL service desk practice in large organisations, 2019 to 2022.

steps.name: Wait for user (second line)
steps.description: The incident is parked in a wait-user status while the user is out, cannot be reached or must test at a later time. The SLA clock is usually paused, which hides part of the elapsed time from reports.

evidence.note: Wait-user misuse was a question in the Volvo IT challenge and was found to be limited; durations are author estimates.

steps.name: Escalate to third line
steps.description: The second-line engineer writes an escalation note with the evidence gathered and assigns the incident to the application or infrastructure engineering team, sometimes after calling the team lead.

error.defect_description: Escalation note lacks the evidence third line needs.

evidence.note: Escalation from 2nd to 3rd line is described in the BPIC 2013 case. Times are author estimates.

steps.name: Third-line investigation
steps.description: A specialist developer or infrastructure engineer takes the incident from the team queue between project work, investigates code, configuration or capacity, and fixes it directly, prepares a change, or opens a case with the vendor. Recurring faults are linked to a problem record.

next.condition: vendor product defect or vendor-managed service
not a third-line issue, sent back

evidence.note: Third-line and supplier involvement described; branch shares are author estimates.

steps.name: Raise change request for the fix
steps.description: The specialist fills in a change request with the fix, test evidence, back-out plan, risk rating and proposed window, and links it to the incident.

evidence.note: Links between incidents and changes are part of the Rabobank ITIL data; times are author estimates.

steps.name: Record resolution and resolve ticket
steps.description: The resolving engineer writes the resolution notes and closure code, links any problem or change record, and sets the incident to resolved, which notifies the user.

error.defect_description: Thin resolution notes or wrong closure code, which weakens reporting and knowledge reuse.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common ITIL service desk practice in large organisations, 2019 to 2022. Third-line resolutions are often recorded by the specialist; the second-line role is used for simplicity.

steps.name: Wait for user confirmation
steps.description: The user receives the resolution email and can confirm or reject it. Most users do not reply, and the tool closes the ticket automatically after a set number of days; a rejection reopens it.

control.basis: ITSM closure policy: user confirmation or automatic closure after the resolved period

evidence.note: Automatic closure after a configurable number of days is a standard tool setting; three days is an author estimate of a common setting and the reopen rate is an author estimate.

steps.name: Close incident and send survey
steps.description: The scheduled job closes the incident, freezes the SLA measurements and sends a satisfaction survey to a sample of users. Team leads review a sample of closed tickets for quality outside this flow.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common ITIL service desk practice in large organisations, 2019 to 2022.

steps.name: Open vendor support case
steps.description: The specialist opens a case on the vendor's support portal, uploads logs and configuration details, states the business impact and contract severity, and records the vendor case number in the incident.

error.defect_description: Missing logs prompt a vendor request for more data.

evidence.note: Supplier involvement at 2nd and 3rd level is described; the Volvo log includes vendor waits. Times are author estimates.

steps.name: Wait for vendor
steps.description: The incident sits in a wait-vendor status while the vendor analyses the case, asks questions or ships a patch. The specialist chases at intervals and relays updates to the user.

next.condition: patch or configuration change to deploy

evidence.note: Author estimate from common ITIL service desk practice in large organisations, 2019 to 2022.

steps.name: Chase overdue ticket
steps.description: The SLA warning at 50% or 75% of the target alerts the service desk team lead, who checks why the ticket has not been picked up, calls the resolver group lead and pushes for an owner.

evidence.note: SLA notifications at 50%, 75% and breach are stated in the guideline; the share of tickets chased is an author estimate.

steps.name: Declare major incident
steps.description: The major incident manager reviews the impact, confirms the major incident, opens the bridge, pages the on-call engineers and suppliers, and links the incoming user tickets to the parent record.

error.defect_description: Declared late, so users flood the service desk first.

control.basis: Major incident procedure: incident manager declares and leads a temporary major incident team

evidence.note: Declaration criteria and roles are described; times are author estimates.

steps.name: Restore service on the bridge
steps.description: Three to six engineers and vendor staff work the outage on the bridge, check recent changes, fail over or roll back, and apply a workaround to restore service; the touch time is their combined effort.

error.defect_description: Workaround hides the cause, outage recurs.

evidence.note: Operations role and temporary team described; team size and effort are author estimates.

steps.name: Send stakeholder updates
steps.description: The major incident manager sends updates every 30 to 60 minutes to IT leadership, the business and the service desk, and posts the all-clear when service is restored.

evidence.note: Communications role described; frequency is an author estimate.

steps.name: Post-incident review
steps.description: Within about a week the major incident manager collects the timeline, holds a review with the teams involved, writes the report with causes and actions, and hands the root cause to problem management.

control.basis: Major incident procedure: a major incident review follows every major incident

evidence.note: Major incident review is described; timing and effort are author estimates.

steps.name: Approve change for the fix
steps.description: The change manager checks the change record for risk, testing and back-out, consults affected owners, and approves it at the weekly change advisory board or as an expedited change for urgent incidents.

control.basis: IT general controls over change management (for example Sarbanes-Oxley section 404 at listed companies): production changes are authorised before implementation

evidence.note: Author estimate from common ITIL service desk practice in large organisations, 2019 to 2022.

steps.name: Implement fix in change window
steps.description: The specialist deploys the fix in the approved window, often an evening or weekend slot, checks monitoring, and backs it out if the deployment fails.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common ITIL service desk practice in large organisations, 2019 to 2022.

exceptions.name: Major incident
exceptions.description: A widespread outage or loss of a critical service is declared a major incident and handled on a bridge with regular updates and a post-incident review.

exceptions.name: Third-line escalation
exceptions.description: Second line cannot fix the fault and passes it to application or infrastructure engineers.

exceptions.name: Fix needs an approved change
exceptions.description: The fix alters production and waits for change approval and a maintenance window.

exceptions.name: Vendor involvement
exceptions.description: The fault is in a vendor product or vendor-run service and waits on the vendor's support case.

exceptions.name: Reassignment ping-pong
exceptions.description: The incident goes to the wrong group and is passed back or on, adding queue time each hop.

exceptions.name: Reopened after resolution
exceptions.description: The user rejects the resolution or the fault recurs within the confirmation period.

exceptions.name: User stops responding
exceptions.description: The ticket is closed after reminders go unanswered during a wait-user status.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from logging to closed status (includes the resolved-to-closed confirmation period)
benchmarks.population: Internal IT incidents at large organisations (composite estimate)

evidence.note: No opened source reports logging-to-closure times for the reference period. Composite: most incidents are resolved within a working day (Freshservice 2024 average resolution 19.64 hours in one industry; P3 targets of 96 business hours), followed by a resolved period of about three days before automatic closure. The Volvo and Rabobank logs would allow measuring this but their statistics could not be extracted.

benchmarks.unit: share of tickets resolved by the service desk
benchmarks.population: MetricNet benchmark, service desks without and with remote control tools (2017)
MetricNet desktop support benchmark (2018); range 2.7% to 35.1%

benchmarks.unit: hours of end-user work time per extra reassignment
hours (business hours for P3 and P4)
benchmarks.population: One university ITSM default service level

pain_points.description: Incidents are pushed to second line that the service desk could have resolved, raising cost per ticket from about 22 to 91 USD.
Misrouting and reassignment between groups add queue time; each extra reassignment costs users over an hour and a half of work time.
Wait-user and wait-vendor statuses pause SLA clocks, so reported resolution times understate what users experience.

evidence.note: The Volvo IT challenge asked whether wait-user was abused.

pain_points.description: Third-line engineers take incidents between project work, so escalated incidents wait a day or more in team queues.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common ITIL service desk practice in large organisations, 2019 to 2022.

pain_points.description: Fixes that need a production change wait for the weekly change board and a maintenance window.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common ITIL service desk practice in large organisations, 2019 to 2022.

assumptions: Touch time for the affected user covers only replies and tests with IT; the user's lost work time (about two to three hours per incident in end-user surveys) is not modelled as touch time.
A major incident is modelled as one case; the many user tickets linked to it are separate cases resolved at s15 when service returns.
Major incidents are 0.3% of incidents (about six a month at this volume), an author estimate.
Waits are calendar time including nights and weekends; group queues for P3 and P4 incidents often span overnight.
The confirmation period before automatic closure is about three days; organisations set anywhere from one to ten days.

The BPI Challenge 2013 and 2014 logs were used for the flow variants (support lines, wait-user and wait-vendor statuses, links to changes) but not for timings, because their statistics could not be read from the published PDFs.
Loaded hourly cost = BLS May 2021 median wage x 1.42 benefits factor (ECEC December 2021) x 1.15 overhead factor.
The Freshservice resolution time comes from 2024 data outside the reference period and is used only as an order-of-magnitude check.

Simulated labour cost (about 83 USD per incident, touch time only) is above a MetricNet-based blended figure of about 55 USD (22 USD at level 1, plus 69 USD desktop support and 104 USD level 3 for escalated tickets). The gap comes mainly from second- and third-line application and infrastructure time and major incidents, so those touch times should be read as upper-middle estimates.
